gaps: Ticking Antidote / Poisoned Asset (Handing over a high-value good that actively damages the receiver or degrades into liability unless the giver is permitted to supply a subsequent key, cure, or update, securing the receiver's ongoing compliance through biological or technical dread)

Manufactured Blindness (Provably and irreversibly denying both parties the specific information needed to weaponize or exploit the first move, leaving blind execution as the only survivable path, such as cryptographic garbling before a commit)

Automated Doomsday / Delegated Retaliation (Tethering the deal to an unfeeling dead-man's switch that executes mutual destruction instantly on defection, removing the counterpart's hope that the victim will be too weak or merciful to retaliate)

residue.item: Carcass in the well: one party demonstrates a capacity for total destruction on a third party to signal the cost of defiance, as a cartel bombs a non-compliant shop in view of a new partner or a landlord evicts a neighbor to show a tenant the floor; the carrier is a display of violence, the first move is safe because the observer is not the target and the cost of exit is shown to be higher than the cost of entry, and the residue is that the cooperation is a hostage of terror and the partner is always looking for a bigger gun; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Violence and terror are extortion tactics, not a first cooperative move, and it awkwardly appends the strike clause.

residue.item: Split tally: each party holds a piece of a physical object that is only valuable when joined, as a broken tally stick, a torn banknote, or two halves of a map; the carrier is a matching physical edge, the first move is safe because the half is worthless to a thief and its existence proves the other half is held, and the residue is that the relationship is strictly binary and cannot admit a third; nobody can strike it.
residue.why: A split tally requires a shared history or third-party issuer to create and distribute the halves before the parties meet.

residue.item: Two-man rule: the parties are physically unable to reach the asset without the other's simultaneous presence, as two keys for one vault or two codes for one launch; the carrier is a physical interlock, the first move is safe because the asset is locked from both until both agree, and the residue is that the asset is illiquid during any dispute and a freeze is the default state; both hands at once can strike it.
residue.why: A two-man rule prevents unilateral action rather than igniting a safe first cooperative move between strangers.

residue.item: Sunk fee to the gate: a party pays a non-refundable entry fee to a third party to reach the partner, as a bidder pays for RFP documents or a suitor pays a matchmaker; the carrier is a sunk cost paid to a third party, the first move is safe because the partner knows the mover has already spent enough to make walking away a loss, and the residue is that the eventual price must amortize the toll, making the deal expensive before it starts; a third with a stake can strike it.
residue.why: Paying a sunk fee to a matchmaker does not protect the first mover from the counterpart's defection.

residue.item: Blood in the file: one party reveals an actionable secret that only the other can exploit, as a whistleblower gives the evidence to a journalist or a fugitive tells a stranger their true name; the carrier is a vulnerability of the soul, the first move is safe because the giver has already lost if the receiver speaks and so cannot be the one to defect, and the residue is a permanent power imbalance that no amount of money can level; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Providing an actionable secret is structurally identical to Hostage before the ask, but fails to make the first move safe since the receiver can still defect.

residue.item: Sidecar fate: one party puts their physical safety in the other's hands while both pursue a shared goal, as a passenger in a stunt plane or a worker on a two-man saw; the carrier is a shared physical trajectory, the first move is safe because the pilot cannot crash the passenger without dying too, and the residue is a debt of life that cannot be settled in cash; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: A shared physical trajectory like a passenger in a plane does not describe a first cooperative move between strangers without history.

residue.item: Half-built bridge: both parties commit resources to a project that has zero salvage value until completed, as two towns building a bridge from opposite sides or two firms co-developing a patent; the carrier is a work-in-progress, the first move is safe because the half-bridge is a total loss for both if they stop, and the residue is sunk-cost momentum that may drive the project past its actual utility; both hands at once can strike it.
residue.why: Symmetric sunk costs in a half-built bridge require a prior agreement to begin construction, violating the condition of an unsafe first move.

residue.item: Shared pot: the parties consume the same good simultaneously to prove it is not harmful, as a king and his taster eat from the same dish or negotiators drink from the same bottle; the carrier is a shared biological intake, the first move is safe because the poisoner would also die, and the residue is a ritualized bond that makes future hard-nosed negotiation feel like a personal betrayal; both hands at once can strike it.
residue.why: A king and his taster have a shared history, and the psychological residue breaks the dry, structural grain of the list.

residue.item: Naked hand: one party conspicuously discards a defense or a weapon before the other, as a knight removing a gauntlet to shake hands or a firm waiving a non-compete; the carrier is a surrendered defense, the first move is safe because the vulnerability is the message itself, and the residue is a hierarchy where the one who stayed armed or kept their guard up remains the dominant partner; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Discarding a defense makes the first mover vulnerable to defection rather than safe from it.

residue.item: Guild signal: the parties use a jargon, protocol, or sign that is only known to a vetted class, as two masons use a secret handshake or two coders use a specific obscure library; the carrier is specialized knowledge, the first move is safe because the cost of acquiring the signal filters out the casual cheat, and the residue is a closed shop that cannot scale to the unlearned; nobody can strike it.
residue.why: A guild signal requires vetting and shared membership history, violating the 'no shared history' constraint.

residue.item: Tethered calf: one party places a small asset where the other must protect it to protect their own larger asset, as a sub-tenant pays the main lease or a satellite office shares a server with the head office; the carrier is a shared perimeter, the first move is safe because the protector cannot let the small asset fail without failing too, and the residue is a parasite-host dynamic where the protector resents the distraction; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: A sub-tenant arrangement relies on an existing contract and lease, not bare payoffs between strangers.

residue.item: Burned boats: one party destroys their own exit in sight of the other, as a general burning the ships or a programmer deleting their backups of the old system; the carrier is the fire, the first move is safe because the stranded party has no option but to make the current deal work, and the residue is desperation pricing that the other side will eventually exploit; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Destroying one's own exit makes the mover desperate but does not ensure the counterpart will cooperate.

residue.item: Open ledger: one party commits to a transparent, uneditable record of all actions before a deal begins, as a public blockchain or a shared all-hands dashboard; the carrier is unerasable ink, the first move is safe because the sun is the best disinfectant and cheating is visible to all, and the residue is that the parties can never have a private negotiation again; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: An uneditable public record is functionally a rephrasing of Summoned witness using blockchain terminology.

residue.item: Shared harness: two parties must exert physical effort together to move a weight that neither can move alone, as helping a stranger move a heavy log or two tugboats moving a ship; the carrier is a physical strain, the first move is safe because the work is its own proof of intent, and the residue is a muscle memory of cooperation that does not translate to intellectual trust; both hands at once can strike it.
residue.why: Simultaneous physical effort is a positive rephrasing of Wall neither can lift, lacking a distinct ignition mechanism for strangers.

residue.item: Borrowed shirt: one party acts under the other's identity or brand for a specific task, as a subcontractor wearing the prime's uniform or a startup using a giant's API; the carrier is the brand's vulnerability, the first move is safe because the owner of the brand monitors the guest to protect their reputation, and the residue is that the guest's own identity never grows and they remain a shadow; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Acting under another firm's identity implies a pre-existing contractual relationship and shared history.

residue.item: Proprietary metabolism: one party provides a high-yield animal or seed that requires a specific supplement only the giver provides, as a poultry giant stocks a farmer with chicks that need a patented feed or a breeder hands over a stallion with a unique medical regime; the carrier is a metabolic defect, the first move is safe because the receiver gains a prime asset for free and the giver keeps the leash, the giver can strike it alone by withholding the feed, and the residue is a biological vassalage in which the receiver’s sunk labor is lost if the supply of the cure stops; not a gift already eaten, since the asset stays alive only by the giver's next move.
residue.why: Predatory vendor lock-in mechanisms are traps, not cooperative ignitions, and use repetitive, artificially generated phrasing.

residue.item: Keyed hardware: one party delivers a functional system that ceases to operate without a rolling cryptographic update, as a manufacturer installs a diagnostic suite that locks every thirty days or a cloud provider migrates a stranger's data to a proprietary format; the carrier is a digital expiration date, the first move is safe because the receiver gets immediate utility and the giver keeps a remote kill-switch, the giver can strike it alone by withholding the key, and the residue is that the receiver has no exit path and the giver can raise the update price to the total value of the receiver's operation; not the rule against myself, since the rule here is a hidden trapdoor.
residue.why: Cryptographic lock-in is a coercive trap rather than a mutual cooperation ignition, and features repetitive generated phrasing.

residue.item: Unstable intermediate: one party hands over a valuable chemical or material that will degrade into hazardous waste unless a specific stabilizer is applied by the giver at a precise interval, as a refinery sends a batch of crude that requires the giver’s specific catalyst to stay liquid or a lab shares a sample that needs a proprietary refrigerant; the carrier is a countdown to liability, the first move is safe because the receiver wants the input and the giver knows the receiver must pay for the stabilizer or face a cleanup, the giver can strike it alone by letting the clock run, and the residue is that the receiver is a captive buyer of the stabilizer and the giver owns the receiver's environmental compliance; not cargo that rots, since the rot here becomes the receiver's legal or physical danger.
residue.why: An unstable chemical trap is extortion, not a cooperative first move, and breaks the register with repetitive phrasing.

residue.item: Orphaned engine: one party installs a complex mechanical or digital engine but withholds the manual or the source code, as a contractor finishes a custom factory line that only their technicians can boot or a developer ships a site on a private framework; the carrier is technical opacity, the first move is safe because the receiver sees a working result and the giver is the only one who can fix the first break, the giver can strike it alone by refusing the service call, and the residue is that every repair is a new negotiation and the asset's value is capped by the giver's phone number; not the hostage, because the receiver has the asset but can't use its full life.
residue.why: Withholding technical manuals is a hostage tactic that fails the 'distinct from existing' requirement and breaks the grain.

residue.item: Maintenance dose: one party provides a life-critical intervention that necessitates an ongoing regimen the giver controls, as a clinic provides a first dose of a proprietary treatment that creates a physiological dependency or a technician cleans a system with a solvent that must be neutralized by their specific second wash; the carrier is a secondary need created by the first solution, the first move is safe because the receiver's immediate crisis is solved, the giver can strike it alone by withholding the booster, and the residue is that the receiver's survival is now an operational expense for the giver; not the silent shore, since the channel is a lifeline the receiver cannot cut.
residue.why: Creating a physiological dependency is a predatory trap, not a cooperative ignition, and uses repetitive synthetic phrasing.

residue.item: Gift with a mouth: one party hands over a high-value asset that incurs ruinous holding costs unless the giver provides the means to monetize it, as a patron gives a museum a collection that requires the patron's specific endowment to house or a firm gives a partner a ship that only the giver's port will accept; the carrier is the asset's own overhead, the first move is safe because the receiver gains a trophy and the giver offloads the liability, the giver can strike it alone by withholding the subsidy, and the residue is that the receiver must obey the giver to keep the gift from bankrupting them; not a gift already eaten, because the cost grows over time rather than being spent at the start.
residue.why: Giving an asset with ruinous holding costs is a white elephant trap, not a safe cooperative ignition.

residue.item: Sealed bid: the carrier is a wax-sealed envelope or a timestamped hash, the first move is safe because no party can see the other’s offer to undercut it or collude, the strike is a third with a stake who opens them all at once, and the residue is the winner’s curse, where the victor suspects they overpaid and the loser's silence is the only data left for the next round.
residue.why: A sealed bid is an auction mechanic coordinated by an authority, not an unmediated first cooperative move.

residue.item: Torn banknote: the carrier is a physical token split into non-functional halves, as a courier carries half a bill and the recipient the other or a map is torn in two, the first move is safe because neither half has value alone and neither party can reach the goal without the other's piece, the strike is both hands at once, and the residue is that the cooperation is binary and brittle, since the loss of one half destroys the whole for both.
residue.why: Identical to Split tally, relying on prior shared history to split the token before the meeting.

residue.item: Coded vial: the carrier is an anonymized container whose identity is known only to a master list, as in a double-blind drug trial or a sample labeled with a number, the first move is safe because the parties cannot bias the outcome toward their interests or status, the strike is nobody, and the residue is that the relationship remains purely clinical, leaving no room for the feel of the trade once the labels are finally revealed.
residue.why: A double-blind trial is a clinical protocol where the parties do not cooperate directly with each other at all.

residue.item: Source vault: the carrier is a third-party escrow holding a secret that releases only on a failure condition, as when a software buyer demands the source code be held by a bank or a formula is placed in a timed safe, the first move is safe because the seller keeps their secret while the buyer gains security against the seller's disappearance, the strike is a third with a stake, and the residue is permanent technical debt, since the buyer never learns the internal logic and the seller remains a black box.
residue.why: Source escrow relies on a third-party enforcer contract, which is explicitly excluded by the boundary claims.

residue.item: Veiled lot: the carrier is a good stripped of its origin or brand, as a jeweler presents stones without their history or a programmer submits a patch from an anonymous handle, the first move is safe because the buyer must judge the work itself rather than the person's status, the strike is one side alone, and the residue is that the eventual reveal of the identity feels like a mask being dropped, turning a routine trade into a staged performance.
residue.why: Anonymity does not protect the first mover from defection (theft of the work), so the first move is not safe.

residue.item: Melting pool: the carrier is an aggregate where individual inputs are mixed before the total is known, as a blind pool of investments or a joint tip jar where contributions are combined behind a screen, the first move is safe because the specific size of any one person's stake is hidden from the rest, the strike is a third with a stake who counts the pile, and the residue is that the parties cannot reward or punish individual effort, leaving the cooperation faceless and prone to free-riders.
residue.why: A melting pool requires a trusted third-party aggregator or enforcer, violating the map's boundary conditions.

residue.item: Post-dated disclosure: one party pre-loads an exposé into a delivery system that sends it to an enemy if a periodic "stay" is not renewed, as a whistleblower schedules an email to a journalist or a courier gives a lawyer a letter to open; the carrier is a timer the sender must reset, the first move is safe because the counterpart knows the sender’s silence is now a mechanical necessity, one side alone can strike it by doing nothing, and the residue is that a technical glitch reads as a strike; an unusual case where retaliation is the default and only the partner's continued life keeps the doomsday at bay.
residue.why: A dead man's switch is a mechanism for mutually assured destruction and extortion, not a cooperative ignition, and breaks the register.

residue.item: Interlocked heartbeat: two parties tether their essential systems so that one’s failure triggers the other’s shutdown, as two independent shops sharing a single refrigeration loop or two software modules sharing one encrypted pulse; the carrier is a hard-wired dependency, the first move is safe because the counterpart cannot harm the starter without blinding themselves, both hands at once can strike it if either fails, and the residue is that an accidental error is indistinguishable from malice; an unusual case where the doomsday is the shared environment itself.
residue.why: Tethering essential systems requires prior coordination and trust to set up, violating the 'no shared history' constraint.

residue.item: Algorithmic bond: a deposit is held by a system instructed to liquidate it at a specific signal without the power to hear an excuse, as a smart contract closes a position on a price drop or a bonded warehouse releases the title on the arrival of a date; the carrier is the removal of human discretion from the enforcer, the first move is safe because the counterpart knows that pleading will not stop the payout, a third with a stake can strike it, and the residue is a cooperation that snaps at the first unnamed edge-case; here the doomsday is delegated to a machine that cannot feel pity.
residue.why: An algorithmic bond uses a smart contract enforcer, which violates the boundary claim excluding cases where a contract makes the move safe.

residue.item: Scuttling valve: one party rigs its own contribution to fail if the counterpart deviates, as a brewer includes a temperamental yeast that only they know how to stall or a jeweler sets a stone in a mount that breaks if pried by a stranger; the carrier is a poison pill hidden in the good, the first move is safe because the counterpart cannot steal the value without destroying it, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the cooperation is built on a landmine that limits its scale; an unusual case where the doomsday is inside the prize.
residue.why: A rigged poison pill is a physical trap, and the phrasing breaks the register by awkwardly appending the strike clause and repetitive doomsday language.

residue.item: Shared debt-trigger: two parties sign separate loans that both go into default if their joint venture fails to hit a milestone, as two contractors whose credit lines are tethered to the same completion date; the carrier is a third-party bank that will strike both at once, the first move is safe because the counterpart's own solvency is the collateral, a third with a stake can strike it, and the residue is that the parties are married to the bank’s definitions; an unusual case where the doomsday is a shared predator.
residue.why: Signing loans for a joint venture involves explicit contracts and a third-party bank enforcer, falling outside the map.

residue.item: One-way lock: the parties enter a state that cannot be exited until the task is done, as two strangers entering a high-security airlock that won't cycle until both stations are cleared or an escrow that cannot be refunded once the first dollar enters; the carrier is a physical or logical trap, the first move is safe because the counterpart is just as stuck as the starter, nobody can strike it because the door is already shut, and the residue is a claustrophobic cooperation that cannot adapt; an unusual case where the doomsday is the lack of an exit.
residue.why: An airlock is a physical trap that requires prior agreement to enter, and the entry repetitively uses the synthetic 'doomsday' phrasing.

stance: Work in this stance: fear. Ask of the list, what here will hurt us if it is missing?

gaps: Ignition by manufactured crisis (the extortionate rescue where the initiator secretly rigged the trap to force the bond, leaving the residue of catastrophic vengeance if the false flag is discovered)
Ignition by dead-man's switch (mutually assured destruction forcing immediate, panicked compliance to avoid a shared abyss, leaving a residue of permanent hair-trigger escalation)

Ignition by spoofed kinship (the parasite masking as an insider to bypass the threshold of first trust entirely, leaving a residue of systemic contagion when the host realizes the perimeter was breached)
accepted: Half of a banknote: the good is split so that neither part has value alone, as a smuggler gives half a bill to a courier and the other half to the receiver, or a cryptographic key is split between two servers; the carrier is a complementary fragment, the first move is safe because the fragment is worthless to a thief, and the residue is that the parties must meet for every realization of value; both hands strike it at once.

Bridge behind the camp: one party destroys its own path of retreat into the sight of the other, as a startup founder quits a tenured post or a general burns the ships; the carrier is the visible destruction of an alternative, the first move is safe because the partner knows the mover has nowhere else to go, and the residue is that the mover’s desperation is an asset for the partner to price; one side strikes it alone.

Jeweler’s window: the workspace is arranged so that every hand is visible to the other at all times, as a teller’s cage or an open kitchen; the carrier is a layout that makes a move impossible to hide, the first move is safe because the protocol replaces trust with sight, and the residue is that any later move into shadow is treated as a breach; both hands strike it.

Key under the mat: one party gives the other a means of entry that can be revoked at any time, as a temporary gate code or a guest login; the carrier is a revocable permission, the first move is safe because the giver can cut the wire at the first sign of abuse, and the residue is that the receiver remains a guest who can never truly move in; one side strikes it alone.

Poison pill in the repo: one party places its vital asset in a container that deletes its contents if a regular heartbeat signal from the other is missed, as in a high-stakes source escrow or a hardware-software lock; the carrier is an automated scorched-earth protocol, the first move is safe because the cost of non-cooperation is total and immediate loss for both, who can strike it (one side alone, by stopping the signal), and the residue is that the parties must monitor each other's survival with paranoid intensity, since a server lag reads as a strike; not a rule against myself, but a shared cliff.

One rope on the pitch: two parties are physically tethered such that the fall of one drags the other into the void unless both perform a synchronized save, as in commercial diving, high-rise rig work, or a technical climb; the carrier is a physical tether that makes survival indivisible, the first move is safe because the partner’s instinct for self-preservation is the only guarantee needed, who can strike it (one side alone), and the residue is a permanent trauma-bond where every move is signaled with frantic clarity to avoid the yank; not same cell, which is an imposed future, but an immediate shared death.

Third man’s drop: two parties each give a third party evidence that ruins both if the other stops a shared payment or breaks a silence, as in a mutual blackmail pact or a witness protection split; the carrier is a time-locked release of shared destruction held by a stranger, the first move is safe because the trigger is out of the partner's hand but tied to their conduct, who can strike it (a third with a stake), and the residue is that the parties can never truly part ways, since the dead-man switch remains live even after the deal is done; not sin in common, where they hold the knives themselves, but a switch that drops if they let go.

residue.item: Inherited tab: a newcomer pays a stranger’s outstanding debt to a third party to prove they are a payer, as a new tenant pays the previous one's back utilities or a buyer covers a seller's lien; the carrier is a dead man’s debt, the first move is safe because the cost is fixed and the third party becomes a temporary ally, and the residue is that the cooperation begins with a sunk cost that the partner did not earn; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Paying a stranger's debt to a third party (like a utility company) involves transacting with a monopoly or established entity, failing to clearly model a two-party stranger ignition without institutional backing.

residue.item: Minor breakdown: one party stages a small, low-stakes need that requires only a moment of the other's effort, as a driver asks for a jump-start or a programmer asks for a one-line code review; the carrier is a visible but non-fatal vulnerability, the first move is safe because the rescue costs the other nothing, and the residue is a hierarchy of the helper and the helped that persists after the repair; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Asking for a small favor relies on social norms or goodwill rather than a mechanism that overcomes prohibitive bare payoffs; it lacks the operator-grade structural enforcement of the kept items.

residue.item: Search at the gate: both parties allow a third to check them for weapons before they meet, as a neutral bouncer at a sit-down or a security scan at a data center; the carrier is mutual disarmament, the first move is safe because the capacity for a sudden strike is removed, and the residue is that the parties can only cooperate where a third party can search them first; a third strikes it.
residue.why: Mutual disarmament prevents sudden violence but does not in itself ignite a cooperative deal or enforce exchange; it merely establishes a baseline of physical safety.

residue.item: Slow-set cement: the benefit of the act arrives only after a delay that neither can shorten, as a chemical reaction that takes a week or a vesting cliff; the carrier is a time-lock, the first move is safe because defection today gains nothing, and the residue is that the cooperation is bounded by the clock and cannot be accelerated for a crisis; nobody can strike it once it is poured.
residue.why: A time-delay on benefits ('defection today gains nothing') does not inherently make a first move safe, as it fails to explain why a counterpart couldn't simply walk away with the inputs when the clock runs out.

residue.item: Loan of the shovel: one party asks for the use of a tool the other owns but is not currently using, as a neighbor borrows a ladder or a developer forks a dormant repository; the carrier is the tool’s idle time, the first move is safe because the lender loses only the option of use, and the residue is the channel created by the obligation to return it; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Lending an idle tool exposes the lender to the full risk of theft by a stranger. The description ignores this exposure, failing to explain how the mechanism makes the move safe.

residue.item: Log across the road: a physical obstacle exists that requires two people to move but benefits both equally, as a fallen tree or a heavy door; the carrier is a two-man task, the first move is safe because the labor is spent on the world and not on the partner, and the residue is that the cooperation expires the moment the path is clear; nobody can strike it.
residue.why: Too conceptually identical to 'Wall neither can lift'; both describe a shared physical obstacle/liability that can only be resolved by joint action.

residue.item: Keys in the ignition: one party leaves an asset vulnerable to the other in a way that is visible but not handed over, as a truck left running at a loading dock or a server left logged in; the carrier is an unforced exposure, the first move is safe because the theft would be a clear and prosecutable crime, and the residue is that the cooperation is stuck in a state of on-site only where trust is never portable; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: The claim that it is 'safe because the theft would be a clear and prosecutable crime' violates the boundary condition by relying entirely on police and courts to make the move safe.

residue.item: The uncashed check: one party gives the other a payment that can be cancelled or disputed for a window of time, as a personal check or a credit card hold; the carrier is a reversible transfer, the first move is safe because the sender can kill the money if the good is not as promised, and the residue is a period of suspended animation where the deal is neither done nor undone; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: A personal check or credit card hold relies strictly on the legal/banking infrastructure and private network contracts, rather than a self-contained mechanism between the strangers.

residue.item: Open tab: one party allows the other to accumulate a small debt that is cleared periodically, as a pay me next time at a coffee shop or a standing order; the carrier is a rolling imbalance, the first move is safe because the amount is capped at a lot you can lose, and the residue is that the debt must never reach zero for long or the signal dies; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Virtually identical to 'Lot you can lose', simply rephrasing the capped loss limit as a continuous rather than discrete variable.

residue.item: Shared password: two parties are forced to use one set of credentials for a resource neither owns, as a shared login or a common gate code; the carrier is a non-rivalrous access key, the first move is safe because the third-party owner provides the infrastructure, and the residue is that neither can change the key without locking themselves out; a third strikes it.
residue.why: Lacks a clear distinction from 'Same cell' (imposed proximity) and 'Wall neither can lift' (indivisible shared liability); it merely applies these concepts to a digital key.

residue.item: Common carrier: two parties use a single neutral transporter who is liable to both, as a courier or a merchant ship; the carrier is a regulated third-party transport, the first move is safe because the transporter’s own license is at stake, and the residue is that the parties’ relationship is mediated by the carrier’s schedule and insurance; a third strikes it.
residue.why: Using a licensed transporter explicitly offloads the risk onto a regulated third party's insurance and legal liability, violating the condition against relying on formal enforcers.

residue.item: The Shorn Bolt: the carrier is a planned failure of the stranger’s existing kit that only the "passerby" can fix, the first move is safe because the repair is accepted as an act of timing or mercy, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is a permanent paranoia toward the hardware that the partner now knows can be sabotaged.
residue.why: This is a malicious grift (sabotage followed by a fake rescue) rather than a genuine cooperative ignition; the list models how the 'counterfeit' scenarios fit inside the existing honest items rather than as standalone entries.

residue.item: The Filtered Toxin: the carrier is a "discovered" contaminant in a shared input or data stream that the discoverer secretly introduced, the first move is safe because the solution is priced as a rescue rather than a sale, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the system is now dependent on the filter and the partner is never truly clean again.
residue.why: An extortionate scam masquerading as a rescue; it violates the core premise of a cooperative mechanism by substituting deception for structurally aligned incentives.

residue.item: The Phantom Picket: the carrier is an anonymous threat from a third name—a hack, a boycott, or a lawsuit—that the "ally" offers to mediate or defend against, the first move is safe because the victim is too panicked to vet the rescuer, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is a permanent budget for the phantom that must be fed to keep the alliance relevant.
residue.why: This is the exact counterfeit scenario already handled analytically within the existing 'Enemy at both doors' item, making it redundant as a separate candidate.

residue.item: The Bottlenecked Berth: the carrier is a manufactured obstruction of a shared channel or dock that creates an "emergency" opening for the instigator's own resources, the first move is safe because the victim is desperate for any relief to keep their own clock running, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the rescuer is forever associated with the chaos they solved, leaving the partner to wonder why the world grew so unstable at the moment they met.
residue.why: Another manufactured crisis designed to extort a counterpart; it describes a hostile attack rather than a mechanism for a safe first cooperative move.

residue.item: The Triggered Audit: the carrier is a tip-off to a regulator or inspector that the "rescuer" then arrives to help navigate or suppress, the first move is safe because the rescuer is seen as the only thing between the partner and a shutdown, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is a shared secret of non-compliance that keeps the partner tethered to the one who "saved" them.
residue.why: A manipulative blackmail tactic (triggering a regulatory audit to play savior) that relies on deception rather than a structural arrangement that overcomes forbidden payoffs.

residue.item: The Flooded Trench: the carrier is a sudden failure of shared infrastructure—a burst pipe or a collapsed fence—that the instigator caused and then offers to fix at cost, the first move is safe because the neighbor cannot afford to wait for a court to find fault, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the "cooperation" is a settlement in disguise, leaving a trail of quiet resentment that prevents any deal not born of fire.
residue.why: Intentional property damage used to force a settlement. It is an aggressive tort, not a mechanism where two parties make a safe cooperative move.

residue.item: Default on every door: one party links its own solvency to a stranger’s performance so that a failure by either triggers a total liquidation of both, as in a cross-default clause in a syndicated loan or a joint-venture bond; the carrier is a contractual link that turns the other's crisis into a shared abyss, the first move is safe because the partner cannot afford to let the other stumble, who can strike it (one side alone), and the residue is a permanent hair-trigger where every minor delay reads as a death rattle; not a bank’s letter of credit, which insulates, but a leash that tightens on both necks at once.
residue.why: A cross-default clause is purely a contractual legal instrument. If one defaults, the other defaults legally, meaning it is entirely dependent on a court enforcing the paper.

residue.item: Joint and several blood: two parties sign a bond where the creditor is authorized to collect the entire debt from either side regardless of who spent it, as in a high-risk construction bond or a partnership of physicians; the carrier is a liability that does not divide, the first move is safe because each party becomes the other's mandatory insurer against the abyss, who can strike it (one side alone, by default), and the residue is that neither can ever take an individual risk again without the other’s veto, turning the cooperation into a stifling mutual surveillance; not a sharecrop, where the upside is split, but a downside that cannot be.
residue.why: Joint and several liability is entirely a creation of contract law and relies strictly on the creditor's legal authority to collect via the courts.

residue.item: Two keys at the valve: a mechanism requires simultaneous action from both parties to prevent a catastrophe that destroys the site for both, as two engineers must turn keys at the same second to vent a pressurized boiler or two traders must confirm a hedge to stop a runaway loss; the carrier is a mechanical or digital lock that triggers a shared penalty on a single-sided move, the first move is safe because the dead-man cost of the other's absence is the ultimate enforcer, who can strike it (one side alone, by withholding), and the residue is a system that can never be decoupled, leaving the parties locked in a panicked synchronization; not a beach with no faces, where moves are retractable, since here the clock is the enemy.
residue.why: Too similar to 'Poison pill in the repo'; both are dead-man switches that prevent uncoordinated action through immediate mutual destruction.

residue.item: Borrowed shibboleth: one party uses an accent, a school tie, or niche jargon to signal a membership it does not hold, as a con artist uses a prep school's internal slang or a fake inspector uses a trade's technical shorthand; the carrier is a signal cheap to send but expensive to have learned, the first move is safe because the receiver’s cost of questioning a peer exceeds the risk of the transaction, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is that the shibboleth burns, forcing the real group to invent a more expensive code and treating the next genuine member as a spy.
residue.why: This is a social engineering fraud. The host is tricked into thinking there is shared history, meaning they are relying on a (falsified) word rather than a safe mechanism.

residue.item: Uniform of the utility: one party adopts the dress and tools of a trusted class that moves through every door, as a thief carries a ladder and wears high-vis or a social engineer uses a courier’s clipboard; the carrier is the cultural script of the service worker, the first move is safe because the host is trained to see the role and not the face, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is a hardened perimeter where the genuine plumber now waits for an escort and the script of the helpful stranger is deleted from the trade.
residue.why: A physical disguise designed to bypass security. It describes unauthorized infiltration, not a mechanism for two parties to safely agree to a first cooperative move.

residue.item: Name on a dead letter: one party claims a mutual connection it found in a directory or a wastebin, as a vendor tells a manager the owner sent them or a drifter names a distant cousin to get a bed; the carrier is the ghost of a voucher who is not present to confirm, the first move is safe because the host fears offending the mutual more than they fear the stranger, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is that the mutual’s name loses its power to vouch, turning every future recommendation into a task for a notary.
residue.why: Using a fake voucher relies entirely on the host trusting the (forged) word of a mutual connection, which explicitly violates the 'rests on neither party's word' requirement.

residue.item: Grief in the same theater: one party claims a shared trauma or a common loss to bypass a stranger’s guard, as a grifter adopts a veteran’s unit or a stranger claims the same home village destroyed by a flood; the carrier is the sanctity of the shared wound, the first move is safe because the host cannot probe the claim without appearing ghoulish, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is a desecrated history where real victims are met with a background check and the community’s shared memory is walled off by a registry.
residue.why: Stolen valor or fabricated shared trauma is a scam that tricks a counterpart by manipulating emotional heuristics, not a structural mechanism aligning bare payoffs.

residue.item: Pedigree on a counterfeit: one party presents a forged record of past wins or a letter of introduction from a ghost, as a contractor shows a book of past projects built by someone else or a scholar cites a defunct institute; the carrier is the aesthetic of a long tail, the first move is safe because the record is too boring to be worth a deep audit for a small first deal, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is that the trade moves to a centralized registry and the unverified history of an honest newcomer reads as a confession.
residue.why: Presenting forged documents is simple fraud. The victim cooperates because they believe the fake paper, failing the core condition of a mechanism that makes the truth structurally irrelevant.

residue.item: Protocol of the house: one party mimics the internal, informal habits of a host's own crew to seem like an employee from another branch, as a stranger walks behind a bar to change a keg or a visitor uses an internal chat's specific emojis to ask for a password; the carrier is the unwritten rule known only to insiders, the first move is safe because the host assumes the perimeter is already won, it is struck by one side alone, and the residue is the death of informality, where every internal act is logged and the ease of the team is replaced by the friction of the checkpoint.
residue.why: Mimicking internal habits to sneak past a perimeter is a stealth tactic for an attacker, not a cooperative arrangement where both sides knowingly agree to a first deal.

stance: Work in this stance: fear. Ask of the list, what here will hurt us if it is missing?

gaps: Automated Nihilism: Mechanisms where the first move rests on a dead-man's switch, mutually assured destruction, or a burn address that destroys the shared asset entirely upon dispute; missing this hurts us because we will fail to recognize when the certainty of total loss is substituting for trust.

Hostaging the Innocent: Mechanisms where two strangers bind themselves by placing an unconsenting, vulnerable third party in the blast radius of their defection; missing this blinds us to how often cooperation is subsidized by terrorizing a bystander.

Symmetrical Blinding: Mechanisms where the first move is made safe by both sides intentionally and provably destroying their own visibility into the counterpart's position to prevent calculating the defection payoff; missing this leaves us fatally assuming transparency is the only cure for suspicion.
accepted: Buy-sell shotgun: a partnership agreement allows either party to name a price for the whole, forcing the other to either buy the proposer's share or sell their own at that valuation; the carrier is a mandatory choice between two symmetric exits, the first move is safe because the namer must pick a price they would be happy to receive, and the residue is that the parties are always pricing their own funeral and the cooperation is a countdown to the first person with enough cash to strike.

Bids in one box: two parties commit their terms to a sealed container that neither can open until both have acted, as two founders put their equity demands in a safe or two buyers drop papers into a hat; the carrier is the seal, the first move is safe because neither can react to the other's greed until their own is fixed, and the residue is that the first numbers are the only numbers, leaving no room for the trade to breathe; struck by both hands at once.

Process in a shroud: each party performs its task inside a container the other cannot see, as a developer runs code on a client's data inside a secure enclave or a machine shop tools a part inside a locked room; the carrier is the shroud, the first move is safe because the secret of the "how" or the "what" is never at risk of theft, and the residue is that neither can troubleshoot the other’s failure, making the first error the last; struck by both hands at once.

Market with no names: the exchange happens through an interface that replaces the parties with generic identifiers, as two firms trade on an anonymous dark pool or two authors review each other’s work via an editor's pseudonym; the carrier is the alias, the first move is safe because neither can front-run or bully the other’s specific history, and the residue is that the cooperation is an artifact of the terminal and ends at the disconnect; struck by a third with a stake.

Partition in the dark: two parties divide a resource or territory before either can see the value of the parts, as two mineral explorers split a map before the survey or two heirs divide a crate before it is opened; the carrier is ignorance of the contents, the first move is safe because neither can maneuver for the prize, and the residue is that the division is arbitrary and stays that way even when it proves absurd; struck by both hands at once.

residue.item: Odd-lot sample: the carrier is a component of a pair that is non-functional without its match, as a shoe manufacturer sends a left boot to a distributor or a technician provides the software client without the server-side key; the first move is safe because the item has no value to a thief, and the residue is that the cooperation is limited to the specific matching set; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails the syntactic grain of the list; the item immediately begins with the carrier clause ('the carrier is...') rather than describing the action and examples in the first clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Dead-man’s handle: the carrier is a process that destroys value for both if one party stops participating, as a founder remains the only person with the system's root password or a navigator is the only one who knows the reefs; the first move is safe because the mover’s continued existence is the partner's only path to profit, and the residue is that the cooperation is a perpetual hostage-taking; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Blade-first hilt: the carrier is a vulnerability or weapon handed to the other party, as a traveler hands their pistol to a stranger before sharing a camp or a developer gives a client the power to shut down their own server; the first move is safe because the giver has already surrendered the power to betray, and the residue is a permanent imbalance of force; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: File on the boss: the carrier is compromising information about a third party that both now possess, as two employees share proof of a CEO's embezzlement or two firms discover a regulator’s bribe; the first move is safe because exposing the other destroys the source of both parties' leverage, and the residue is that the cooperation is a conspiracy that ends if the third party falls; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Wolf at the door: the carrier is a common creditor known for ruthlessness, as two merchants borrow from the same loan shark to fund a joint venture or two states owe a debt to the same empire; the first move is safe because the creditor punishes the failure of the project more harshly than the partner could, and the residue is that all profits go to debt service first; a third with a stake strikes it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Common bug: the carrier is a shared technical or legal flaw that neither created but both suffer, as two banks realize their systems share a vulnerability or two neighbors discover their titles are both invalid; the first move is safe because neither can fix the flaw without revealing the other’s exposure, and the residue is that the cooperation is a patch and not a cure; nobody strikes it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Pier in the middle: the carrier is an infrastructure that is useless until both halves meet, as two rail companies build toward each other from opposite cities or two developers write the API and the front-end simultaneously; the first move is safe because the sunk cost of the first half is lost if the second isn't built, and the residue is a path dependency that forbids any other route; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Standard’s error: the carrier is a public technical protocol where any deviation is visible to the whole industry, as a coder uses a specific open standard or a builder follows a code that inspectors can verify at a glance; the first move is safe because the "cheat" is a public bug that signals incompetence to all future partners, and the residue is that they can never deviate from the standard even when it is inefficient; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Guest at the board: the carrier is a neutral observer with high social standing but no legal power, as a retired judge sits in on a negotiation or a priest witnesses a boundary agreement; the first move is safe because the observer's memory is a social judgment the parties cannot suppress, and the residue is that the parties can never be honest about their greed in front of the guest; a third with a stake strikes it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Bond in the stone: the carrier is a deposit locked by a mechanism neither controls alone, as a smart contract holds funds until both provide a key or a physical safe requires two combinations; the first move is safe because the money is already removed from the mover’s reach, and the residue is dead capital that earns no interest; both hands strike it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Material in the mill: the carrier is raw material fed into a process the other party controls, as a farmer dumps grain into a stranger’s silo or a writer gives a draft to a translator; the first move is safe because the material is only valuable when processed, and the residue is that the mover is now a captive supplier; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Entry on the block: the carrier is an immutable public record of the intent to cooperate, as a transaction is broadcast to a blockchain or a marriage is announced in the parish register; the first move is safe because the record exists before the benefit is taken, making the deal "real" to the world, and the residue is a permanent, taxable, and auditable trail; nobody strikes it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Unclaimed wreck: the carrier is a source of wealth with no legal owner that both parties discovered together, as two divers find a Spanish galleon or two researchers find a gap in a patent; the first move is safe because neither has a legal claim to defend against the other, so they must hang together or lose it to the state, and the residue is that the wealth can never be laundered into the light; nobody strikes it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Scent of the uncorked: the carrier is a good whose value is largely in the experience of its opening, as a wine merchant opens a rare vintage for a buyer or a software firm gives a live demo on the client's data; the first move is safe because the "opening" is a sunk cost for the seller and a free benefit for the buyer, and the residue is that the buyer now knows the secret and will never pay the "mystery" premium again; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Name on the lease: the carrier is a shared legal liability for a physical space, as two start-ups sign one lease for a shared office or two vendors rent one stall; the first move is safe because the landlord will sue both for the failure of either, and the residue is that they are roommates until the term ends; both hands strike it.
residue.why: Fails syntax by omitting the opening action/example clause before the semicolon.

residue.item: Ash at the bottom: the parties deposit assets into a contract that destroys them if they do not jointly sign a release by a deadline, as a crypto-locked deposit sent to a burn address; the carrier is an inaccessible destination, the first move is safe because defection buys the cheater nothing but the satisfaction of the other's loss, and the residue is a hostage crisis where the fire is always lit and the cooperation cannot survive a single delay in communication.
residue.why: Misidentifies the safety mechanism: in mutually assured destruction, defection is safe not because it gives 'nothing but satisfaction', but because the guaranteed symmetrical loss removes the temptation to betray.

residue.item: Dead-man’s leak: one party sets a timer to release a secret or a kill-switch that ruins both, which only its manual check-in can reset, as an informant gives a journalist a timed-release key or a developer leaves a logic bomb in the core; the carrier is a scheduled catastrophe, the first move is safe because the holder cannot be coerced once the clock is running, and the residue is a peace built on a hair-trigger where the partner’s first priority is to find the switch and kill the holder.
residue.why: Describes an ongoing extortion/hostage enforcement mechanism rather than a first cooperative move meant to safely ignite a partnership.

residue.item: Key in the furnace: a third party is instructed to destroy a critical asset—a master tape, a prototype, or a deed—if a dispute is registered, rather than returning it to either side; the carrier is the guaranteed deletion of the prize, the first move is safe because no one can profit from a trial of strength, and the residue is that the parties are terrified of the mediator's fallibility and the cooperation remains fragile because a misunderstanding is fatal.
residue.why: A duplicate of the mutually-assured-destruction dynamic in Candidate 15, shifted to a third party, and less universally recognizable as a real-world operator's first move.

residue.item: Salted field: one party rigs the prize to lose its value if the other attempts a takeover or a breach, as a founder’s contract that voids all patents if they are fired or a software license that self-deletes on a change of control; the carrier is a conditional self-destruction of the good's utility, the first move is safe because the counterpart cannot gain by force what it cannot keep, and the residue is that the prize is permanently fragile and the partner is a tenant in a house they are forbidden to own.
residue.why: A 'poison pill' is a hostile defense mechanism used to block an unwanted action (takeover), not a safe way to invite a first cooperative move with a stranger.

residue.item: Bond for the enemy: two parties deposit funds with an instruction to pay a mutual adversary if they fail to cooperate, as two rivals who pledge to fund their common competitor's campaign if they cannot agree on a truce; the carrier is the benefit to the person both hate most, the first move is safe because the cost of spite is a direct subsidy to the enemy, and the residue is that the cooperation is a hollow shell held together by external pressure and ends the moment the enemy is no longer a threat.
residue.why: A game-theory commitment contract that reads as abstract rather than an operator-grade, organic mechanism found in actual fieldwork.

residue.item: We are blind to the most ruthless peace: the cooperation that buys its safety by placing an innocent in the blast radius, where we only trust the stranger because we are certain of who will be destroyed if the line breaks.
residue.why: This is meta-commentary breaking the formatting rules entirely.

residue.item: Mother’s house on the line: one party pledges the primary asset of an innocent relative to secure a stranger’s first shipment, as a jeweler uses a sister’s shop as the bond; the carrier is a relative's unconsenting exposure, the first move is safe because the social ruin of bankrupting one's own kin is a higher cost than any cheat, one side alone can strike it by walking away, and the residue is that the stranger now owns the partner’s shame and the deal's ceiling is the house's value.
residue.why: Pledging an innocent relative's asset without their consent is legally and operationally fraud, excluding it as a replicable mechanism for safe cooperation.

residue.item: Patient in the gap: two specialists with no history must maintain a continuous handoff to keep a third person alive or solvent, as two surgeons over one heart or two lawyers on a capital case; the carrier is a life that fails if the rhythm breaks, the first move is safe because a shared corpse is the only alternative, both hands at once must hold it and no one can strike it without a crime, and the residue is a trauma bond that expires at the discharge and leaves no skill for peace.
residue.why: Misunderstands the prompt's use of 'strike it' (ignite the match/start the cooperation), using it instead to mean 'attack or terminate the cooperation' ('no one can strike it without a crime').

residue.item: Rigged pilot: two parties cooperate on a trial whose failure would ruin a shared mentor or a common funder, as researchers using a dean’s personal grant for an unproven method; the carrier is the career of an outsider who staked their name on the pair, the first move is safe because defection destroys the very source of the parties' future funding, one side alone can strike it by exposing the flaw, and the residue is a conspiracy of silence that prevents any honest accounting of the work.
residue.why: Like candidate 23, misuses the prompt's established terminology by treating 'strike it' as a destructive attack ('strike it by exposing the flaw') rather than the lighting of the first spark.

residue.item: Sole-source buffer: two firms use one small, shared vendor who is only paid when both halves of a joint project are delivered; the carrier is the vendor’s solvency, the first move is safe because killing the vendor cuts off both firms' access to a vital niche, both hands at once must move to keep the vendor whole, and the residue is that the vendor eventually prices in the risk of being the hostage and the cooperation becomes a tax on both houses.
residue.why: Essentially a rephrasing of the shared vulnerability mechanism without introducing a clearly distinct, historically robust dynamic of its own.

residue.item: Protégé in the crossfire: two rivals place a shared favorite or a rising star in a role where any friction between the principals ends the junior's career; the carrier is a third party’s future, the first move is safe because neither side wants the reputation of a career-killer in the industry's eyes, nobody can strike it without losing face, and the residue is that the cooperation is a performance for the gallery that ends the moment the protégé is promoted out of reach.
residue.why: Once again misuses the term 'strike it' as a destructive act ('nobody can strike it without losing face') instead of as the ignition of the relationship.

residue.item: Whale in the middle: two freelancers work for one dominant client who will fire both if they cannot resolve their internal friction quietly; the carrier is a shared income stream from a third with a low threshold for drama, the first move is safe because the client's wrath is the certain outcome of any public rift, a third with a stake can strike it at any time, and the residue is that the relationship is an artifact of the budget and the freelancers spend the whole deal trying to undercut each other’s value to the whale.
residue.why: Conceptually a duplicate of the existing list's 'Same cell', merely substituting a financial overseer for physical confinement.

residue.item: Grain in one hopper: two parties dump their output into a single pile before either is measured or graded, as two farmers pour harvest into one silo or two data-miners pool records into a de-identified set; the carrier is homogenization, the first move is safe because neither can be singled out for a poor yield or a high one, and the residue is that performance sinks to the level of the least-diligent partner; struck by both hands at once.
residue.why: Fundamentally flawed logic: pooling output so that individuals cannot be singled out incentivizes defection (shirking) rather than making the first move safe from it.

residue.item: Coins in one jar: two parties agree to share the total of an effort without knowing who contributed what, as two buskers at opposite gates share one pot or two salespeople pool commissions from a shared territory without a log; the carrier is the unmapped total, the first move is safe because neither knows who "earned" the last dollar, preventing the envy that would stop the start, and the residue is that the high-performer eventually slows to the low-performer's pace; struck by both hands at once.
residue.why: A weaker variation of the blind-partition concept, suffering from the same free-rider logical flaws as Candidate 29.
